analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal water pollution rules on large factory farms, requiring permits and phasing out open-air waste lagoons.
analysis.headline: Introduced in 1999 with 23 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to a House subcommittee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Water Act to require permits for large concentrated animal feeding operations — industrial-scale livestock and poultry farms. Permits would have mandated water monitoring, recordkeeping, and approved nutrient management plans. It would have required new waste containment standards, banned unlined lagoons within five years and open-air lagoons within ten, limited how and where manure could be spread on land, and made companies that own the animals jointly liable for pollution fines.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near large feedlots and drink from or recreate in affected waters. The bill's findings cite cryptosporidium and Pfiesteria outbreaks linked to animal feeding operations, and it would have required monitoring of both surface water and groundwater, banned aerial manure spraying near homes and wells, and eliminated discharges to streams and groundwater.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents and anyone drinking affected water

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have made it unlawful for a concentrated animal feeding operation to discharge pollutants without a permit, closing a gap in pollution controls the bill's findings called inadequate [S3].
Permits would have required surface and groundwater monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting to verify that no discharge was occurring [S3].

It would have banned unlined waste containment structures within five years and eliminated open-air lagoons for storing animal waste within ten, and required failsafe containment systems for wet waste operations [S3].
Manure application above what crops can absorb would have counted as an illegal discharge, and aerial spraying near residences, wells, and waterways would have been restricted [S3].

Companies holding a controlling or contractual interest in confined animals would have been jointly liable for pollution penalties in proportion to their share of animals, so the corporations behind contract farming could not leave cleanups and fines entirely to the local operator [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large livestock and poultry operations, including the corporations and integrators that own the animals, would bear compliance costs: new lined containment, monitoring, permits, and nutrient management planning. Those costs could show up in meat prices and could push some marginal operations out of business.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs — lined containment, monitoring, permits, and plans — would fall on producers and would likely be passed through to meat and dairy prices, an expense even honest supporters would acknowledge [S3].

The joint liability provision reaches any person with a controlling, contractual, or beneficial interest in a confined animal, including employees and agents, a broad sweep that could have deterred some investment in livestock production [S3].

Strictly phasing out lagoons and requiring costly containment could have accelerated consolidation, squeezing smaller producers out while large integrators absorbed the cost — a real trade-off for farm communities even though the bill aimed to curb industrial-scale pollution [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and water quality case was concrete — the bill cites documented illness outbreaks and fish kills tied to feedlot runoff [S3]. The main cost is higher compliance spending in livestock production, some of it passed to consumers, and a risk of faster consolidation. On balance, a serious effort to address a large, specific pollution source at a cost borne mainly by the industry causing it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative George Miller of California and five other House members introduced the bill on February 10, 1999 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment [S5].
The bill never advanced beyond the subcommittee referral; the record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 106th Congress [S5].
Twenty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large livestock and poultry operations avoided the permitting, monitoring, containment, and liability requirements the bill would have imposed; neighboring residents and waterways gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. George Miller (D-CA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on February 10, 1999.

for.name: 23 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill; none advanced it further.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 10, 1999 and sent it to the Water Resources subcommittee; never acted on it, so no vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats, alongside the Democratic sponsor; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in committee without a vote that would have shown broader party positions.

industries.industry: Large livestock and poultry operations (concentrated animal feeding operations)
industries.note: The bill would have required individual permits, groundwater and surface water monitoring, lined containment, an end to open-air lagoons, and limits on manure spreading — a direct cost to operations that currently store waste in lagoons and apply it to land. These operations profit from practices the bill's findings describe as inadequately controlled sources of water pollution [S3].

industries.industry: Corporate animal owners and livestock integrators
industries.note: Companies with controlling or contractual interests in confined animals would have been jointly liable for pollution penalties in proportion to their share of animals, closing a common structure in which integrators own the animals while contract farmers bear the risk and environmental exposure [S3].

industries.industry: Small farms below the regulatory thresholds
industries.note: Operations under the specified animal capacities (e.g., under 1,000 swine over 55 pounds or 50,000 laying hens) would generally fall outside the permit mandate, though an operation contributing to watershed degradation could still be covered [S3].
